title: The extra surprise tax
allegory: KL divergence is the extra surprise tax you pay, on average, for packing by a wrong forecast Q while the weather really follows P: zero only if the forecast is perfect, and ruinous if it calls real weather impossible.
map: the distribution P that outcomes are drawn from
the distribution Q you compare against
the tax on one day: small if forecast likely, huge if forecast 'almost never'
the extra tax over a perfect forecast, averaged over real days
D_KL(P‖Q) = Σ P(x) log(P(x)/Q(x)) = H(P,Q) − H(P)
a forecast that says 'never' about weather that happens
Q(x) → 0 where P(x) > 0: the KL blows up

cap.1: You pack each morning by a forecast, but the weather does its own thing. How do you score how wrong the forecast is, in one number?
cap.2: Two distributions: what really happens (P) and what a model expects (Q). You want one number for how badly Q describes P, zero only when they match.
cap.3: We want a divergence D(P‖Q) ≥ 0, with equality iff P = Q, that weights each mismatch by how often that outcome actually occurs under P.

cap.1: Each day you pay a surprise tax: tiny if the forecast called that weather likely, huge if it said 'almost never'. KL is the extra a wrong forecast costs.
cap.2: Surprise at outcome x under Q is −log Q(x). Averaged over real days you pay the cross-entropy; a perfect forecast pays only the entropy of P. KL is the gap.
cap.3: D_KL(P‖Q) = H(P,Q) − H(P) = E_P[log P(x) − log Q(x)]: expected excess surprise, in nats with natural logs. Gibbs' inequality makes it ≥ 0, zero iff P = Q.

parts.note: how often day x really happens

cap.1: For every kind of day: how often it really happens, times how much extra surprise the forecast gives it. Add them up. With natural logs the unit is nats.
cap.2: Each term compares log-probabilities on one outcome, weighted by the real frequency P(x). Outcomes P never produces cost nothing, whatever Q says about them.
cap.3: Terms with P(x) = 0 contribute 0; terms with Q(x) → 0 while P(x) > 0 diverge. In code, take log_softmax then exp rather than softmax then log, for stability.

cap.1: It really snows one day in ten. Slide the forecast's snow chance towards zero: one way round the tax keeps climbing, the other way it levels off.
cap.2: Orange, KL(P‖Q), grows without limit as Q(snow) → 0. Blue, KL(Q‖P), stays bounded there. Both are zero where the forecast equals the truth.
cap.3: KL is asymmetric and not a metric: D(P‖Q) diverges as Q(x) → 0 with P(x) > 0; D(Q‖P) does not. Which argument is which is a modelling decision.

chapters.name: Which way round?
chapters.verdict: RLHF uses KL(new ‖ base): no gibberish, but free to drop bad habits.

cap.1: In fine-tuning the old model is the forecaster, reading what the new one writes. Gibberish shocks it and costs a lot; dropping bad habits is free.
cap.2: ARENA's RLHF penalty is kl_coef times KL(new ‖ frozen base). Flip the order and you punish the model for dropping anything the base did, often the whole point of fine-tuning.
cap.3: D_KL(π_θ‖π_ref) is large where π_θ puts mass π_ref lacks, finite where π_θ suppresses π_ref's modes. Reversed args give a plausible, finite number penalising the wrong thing.

chapters.name: One ruler, three jobs
items: VAE: pull each latent cloud towards the prior
RLHF: leash the policy to a frozen base model
Interventions: how much did the output distribution move?

cap.1: The same ruler shows up three times in this course: shaping a VAE, keeping a fine-tuned chatbot close to its base model, and measuring an intervention's effect.
cap.2: It closes the VAE loss, holds an RLHF policy near its reference in [2.4], and in [4.3] measures how much an attention intervention changed a reasoning model's outputs.
cap.3: To steer a model you need to know how far you moved it: KL between output distributions before and after is the standard budget for drift, whether from training or from an intervention.

coda.title: Tune the forecast and watch the extra surprise tax, both ways round

readouts.label: KL(real ‖ forecast)
readouts.f: round(sum([0.6, 0.3, 0.1].map((p, i) => p * log(p / softmax([0, rain, snow])[i]))) * 1000) / 1000 + ' nats'

readouts.label: KL(forecast ‖ real)
readouts.f: round(sum(softmax([0, rain, snow]).map((q, i) => q * log(q / [0.6, 0.3, 0.1][i]))) * 1000) / 1000 + ' nats'

caption.1: Drag snow far left so the forecast says 'never snow'. The first readout climbs, the second barely moves. Then match the real bars to reach zero.
caption.2: KL(real‖forecast) punishes calling real events near-impossible; KL(forecast‖real) punishes expecting what rarely happens. Try rain −0.7, snow −1.8: both hit about 0.
caption.3: Q(x) → 0 with P(x) > 0 sends KL(P‖Q) → ∞ while KL(Q‖P) stays bounded: the asymmetry behind choosing KL(π_θ‖π_ref) as the RLHF penalty.

hamming.what: A number, in nats, for the extra surprise you pay on average by expecting Q when outcomes really follow P.
hamming.when: Whenever one distribution must be compared with or held close to another: a prior, a frozen base model, the same model before an intervention.
hamming.why: It is zero only when the two match and punishes calling real outcomes near-impossible, which is exactly the drift you want to catch.

object.title: The prior's bowl
object.subtitle: Every spot on the floor is a Gaussian cloud; the height is its KL from the standard normal.

knobs.label: Step size for the rolling bead

cap.1: Each spot on the floor is one bell-shaped cloud: left-right is its centre, front-back its width. Height is how far it sits from the standard cloud.
cap.2: x = μ, y = σ of a 1-D Gaussian. Height = KL(N(μ, σ²) ‖ N(0, 1)), the term a VAE adds for every latent dimension.
cap.3: Closed form for Gaussians: KL(N(μ, σ²) ‖ N(0, 1)) = ½(μ² + σ² − 1 − log σ²), summed over dimensions for a diagonal encoder.

cap.1: The lowest point is the standard cloud itself: centre 0, width 1. The height is exactly zero there and nowhere else.
cap.2: KL is zero only when the two distributions are identical, here at μ = 0, σ = 1.
cap.3: The unique minimum at (0, 1) is Gibbs' inequality made visible: D ≥ 0 with equality iff the distributions coincide.

cap.1: Squeeze the cloud thin and the wall shoots up. A cloud much sharper than the standard one pays a lot.
cap.2: As σ → 0 the −log σ² term explodes. This is the pressure that stops a VAE from collapsing back into a plain autoencoder.
cap.3: The −log σ² barrier diverges at σ → 0; without it the encoder goes deterministic and the VAE degenerates to an autoencoder.

cap.1: Slide the centre away from zero and the bowl rises smoothly on both sides.
cap.2: Moving μ costs μ²/2: a gentle parabola, so clouds can spread out but are pulled back towards the middle.
cap.3: The μ term is quadratic and separable from σ, so KL shrinks means towards 0 and widths towards 1 independently.

cap.1: Drop the bead and it rolls to the standard cloud. In a real VAE the rebuild-the-image loss pulls the other way, so clouds settle a bit narrower.
cap.2: Alone, KL drags every cloud to the prior. The reconstruction term pulls σ down, so ARENA suggests printing mean σ and expecting it below 1.
cap.3: Opposing pressures: KL toward (0, 1), reconstruction toward σ → 0. If KL wins outright for every input, that is posterior collapse: z carries no information.

predict.q: The forecast says snow never happens, but it snows one day in ten. What happens to KL(real ‖ forecast)?

options.t: It blows up: every snow day costs the log of almost nothing

predict.why: Each snow day costs −log Q(snow), which grows without limit as Q(snow) goes to zero.

predict.q: RLHF penalises KL(new ‖ base). What can the new model do cheaply?

options.t: Stop saying things the base model often said
Say things the base model finds near-impossible

predict.why: Outcomes the new model never produces get zero weight in the sum, so dropping them costs nothing.

predict.q: Where is this bowl's lowest point?

options.t: At μ = 0, σ = 1, where the cloud equals the prior
At σ = 0, a perfectly sharp cloud

predict.why: KL is zero only when the two distributions are identical; a razor-thin cloud is very far from the prior.
